newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish finmin says no decision taken on EMU punt rate.
newsitem.headline: Irish finmin says no decision taken on EMU punt rate.

text.p: Ireland's finance minister Ruairi Quinn soothed panicked financial markets after the Irish pound plummeted on Wednesday saying no decisions had been taken on the Irish pound rate when entering EMU.

Rumours that the central bank was going to stop intervening to shore up the punt triggered a free-fall in the currency which hit its weakest level against the mark in more than a month and plunging to its lowest level against sterling since August 1993.

"No decision has been taken yet with regards to the rate at which we will join (EMU)," Quinn told Ireland's national broadcaster RTE. "We won't necessarily join at the central rate which is already there and that, I think, is informing some action in the market. The finance ministers have not discussed this," Quinn said.

The Irish unit steadied off immediately after Quinn's comments, recouping a little of its sharp losses against sterling and the mark. By 1600 GMT it nudged up to 0.9230/60 stg and 2.6013/28 marks having hit an intraday low of 0.9153 stg and 2.5759 marks. The punt closed at 0.9485 stg and 2.6705 marks on Tuesday.
Quinn said his intention would be that Ireland join EMU at a rate "... that meets the needs of the Irish economy in the fullest sense of the word" and said he would be looking at how best to do that.

"At the present time, clearly the central rate is at a lower rate than what the market rate is suggesting but there are a lot of positions in between that and we will be looking at all those intermediate positions to see what is in the best interest of the Irish economy," Quinn said.
When asked if he had instructed Ireland's central bank to stop intervening to support the punt Quinn said he had not instructed a change of policy within the central bank.

"Our exchange rate policy is the same as it was enunciated back in March of 1995, that is to trade comfortably within the band," Quinn said. "The responsibility of managing that policy on a day to day basis is a question for the bank as they are responsible for the actions that they take."

The Irish pound succumbed to strong selling pressures which had been building in anticipation of Ireland's perceived desire to enter European Monetary Union (EMU) at the median rate of 2.41 marks early on Wednesday.

Economists said rumours that Ireland's central bank, which had been intervening heavily to shore up the Irish unit in recent weeks, had decided to let the currency fall filtered through the market late on Tuesday.
The rumour opened the floodgates for large volume, mainly foreign, selling of the punt, traders said earlier.

The Irish pound has been hovering near the top of the ERM grid over recent weeks. It has been trading more than 11 percent above the weakest currency within the grid, the French franc, until the punts plunge on Wednesday morning. The Irish unit moved down to 7.37 percent above the French unit by 1056 GMT on Wednesday and moved back up to 8.14 percent above as calm was restored after Quinn's announcement.
